```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_se <- requireNamespace("SummarizedExperiment", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = has_se)
```

This quickstart runs the whole analysis with one call, `rcomplex()`.
It answers one question: which genes keep their co-expression partners
in other species?

## Data

The package ships leaf and root RNA-seq from eight Pooideae grasses.
Each species has 20 leaf samples. We use four species: two annual and
two perennial.

```{r data, message = FALSE}
library(rcomplex)
library(SummarizedExperiment)

se <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "pooideae_vignette.rds",
  package = "rcomplex"
))
leaf <- lapply(
  se[c("BDIS", "BSYL", "HVUL", "HJUB")],
  function(s) s[, s$tissue == "leaf"]
)
```

`rcomplex()` needs two inputs. The first is one expression object per
species, with genes in rows and samples in columns. The second is a
table of hogs: ortholog groups with the columns `species`, `gene` and
`hog`. For an OrthoFinder file, call `read_orthologs()` instead.

```{r hogs}
hogs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(leaf), function(s) {
  data.frame(
    species = s, gene = rownames(leaf[[s]]),
    hog = rowData(leaf[[s]])$hog
  )
}))
head(hogs, 3)
```

## Run

`clades` names the species sets. `null = TRUE` repeats the run with hog
labels shuffled among genes of the same expression level. The run takes
about 10 seconds.

```{r run}
res <- rcomplex(leaf, hogs,
  clades = list(
    annual = c("BDIS", "HVUL"),
    perennial = c("BSYL", "HJUB")
  ),
  null = TRUE, seed = 1
)
res
```

The header lists, per species, the genes, the samples and the density.
The value after "r >=" is the weakest correlation that became an edge. At 20 samples,
a correlation of 0.3 is weak evidence. Read this value first.

The "graphs" line counts the cliques on three gene graphs. The strict
graph holds the calls at `q_value < 0.1`. The loose graph holds the
edges at `q_value < 0.9`. The third graph holds every tested pair, for
the hogs the first two leave without a complete or partial tier.

The last line counts the cliques by tier. A clique is a set of genes,
one per species, that are all co-expressed. A hog with paralogs gives
one clique per gene combination. Paralogs with the same partners are
twins. One clique stands for all their combinations. The line counts
distinct cliques, and the count in brackets includes the combinations.

Gene combinations can explode in a large hog. The clique search keeps
at most `max_cliques` cliques, or copy combinations, per hog (default
100,000). A hog over it
gives one row per group of wired species, with the best copy of each.
`res$capped` lists these hogs.

## Read the results

`summary()` gives the tier table. With `null = TRUE` it also gives the
calls and cliques of the shuffled hog labels.

```{r summary}
summary(res)
```

`calls_null` and `cliques_null` count what abundance and network
structure alone produce. Compare them with `calls` and `cliques`.

`res$edges` has one row per ortholog pair and species pair.

```{r edges}
head(res$edges[, c(
  "gene1", "gene2", "hog", "score", "evalue",
  "q_value", "effect_size", "power"
)], 4)
```

- `score` is `-log2(p)`. Higher is stronger.
- `evalue` is the expected number of pairs this strong by chance.
- `q_value` is the false discovery rate.
- `effect_size` is the fold enrichment of shared partners.
- `power` is the chance to call the pair if it were conserved.

A low `power` means a non-significant pair is weak evidence of
divergence.

`res$classification` has one row per clique. `as.data.frame(res)`
returns the same table. Its `run` column names the graph of the clique.
`partial_significant` comes from the loose graph. `differentiated`
comes mostly from the third graph and needs `clades`.

```{r tiers}
table(as.data.frame(res)$classification)
```

## Save

`write_rcomplex()` writes `edges.tsv`, `cliques.tsv`, `members.tsv`,
`twins.tsv` and `classification.tsv`. After a null run it adds `edges_null.tsv`
and `classification_null.tsv`.

```{r save}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "rcomplex-out")
write_rcomplex(res, out)
list.files(out)
```

## Check the p-value floor

Run `pvalue_resolution()` on any p-values you report. It shows how many
values tie at the floor.

```{r resolution}
pvalue_resolution(res$edges$p_value)
```

## Next steps

- Designed experiment: pass `block` to remove a designed factor.
- Networks built elsewhere: pass `networks = ` to `rcomplex()`.
- Modules: pass `modules = TRUE`.
- Each step alone: see the walkthrough article.
